rationale: reason: "full text not accessible". c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines decentralised rural water governance under Ghana's Community Ownership and Management (COM) model, District Water and Sanitation Plans (DWSPs), Medium Term Development Plans (MTDPs), District Composite Budgets, and the District Monitoring and Evaluation System (DiMES). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, although general asset monitoring and routine physical maintenance Practices would alone resemble operational/project management, the study directly and empirically examines tariff and cost-recovery rules (comparing water point functionality across monthly levy, volumetric pay-as-you-fetch, and no-fixed-tariff / post-paid fix-on-failure regimes in Table 2; assessing volumetric tariff affordability; and evaluating compliance with the 2008 national model bye-law rule requiring small-town WSMTs to pay at least 20% of net monthly revenue into a capital account and CWSA cost-recovery rules splitting OpEx user fees from District Assembly CapManEx support), as well as decentralised service-provider governance structures (WSMTs) and non-enforcement of the CWSA Legislative Instrument (2007).
rationale: Full-text empirical mixed-methods study in rural Ghana examining how tariff and cost-recovery rules (monthly levy vs volumetric pay-as-you-fetch vs no fixed tariff / post-paid fix-on-failure; compliance with the 2008 model bye-law 20% capital-account rule; District Assembly budgeting for CapManEx/ExpDS), decentralized WSMT governance, district monitoring/planning frameworks, and non-enforcement of CWSA Legislative Instrument (2007) affect borehole/handpump and small-town piped water functionality, reliability (>18 days/year downtime), basic service levels, and residents' access to >=20 L/person/day. Satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper arguably touches on an institutional/governance factor—public versus private ownership or operation of community water utilities—though it models utility privatization solely as the dependent variable driven by county demographic traits rather than as an explanatory governance factor; even if Criterion 2 were treated as met under the plain wording, the overall decision remains exclude because Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 fail (no service access outcome is measured). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading ('utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access'), Criterion 2 is 'no' because utility ownership/privatization is the outcome predicted by socioeconomic demographics rather than an exposure or rule-type mechanism empirically tested for its effect on service access.
rationale: Exclude (E04 - Wrong outcome; also reverse exposure-outcome direction under c1/c2). Greiner (2016) conducts a cross-sectional logistic regression of 47,367 U.S. community water systems to identify county-level demographic and socioeconomic predictors (unemployment, household income, racial composition, educational attainment, and population served) of whether a water utility is privately owned or operated. Utility privatization/ownership is modeled strictly as the binary dependent variable rather than as a legal, institutional, or governance exposure governing water access, and no empirical outcome measuring water service access, connection, availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion is reported (tariff increases and water-quality problems are discussed only via secondary literature in the background). Under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain reading of Criterion 2, the study is excluded for lacking a water or sanitation service access outcome.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Under BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, no legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor governing water or sanitation service access is examined. Although the study analyzes rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms—including land/eviction litigation, unauthorized-colony address mapping required for utility metering, electricity privatization (BSES) and anti-theft enforcement, and official surveys and identity/residency documentation for resettlement housing eligibility—these mechanisms are analyzed exclusively in relation to housing and electricity, not water or sanitation. Consequently, both decision and plain_criterion2_decision are exclude.
rationale: Excluded under E07 (Wrong service). Although this empirical ethnographic and survey study investigates how residents and local leaders in unplanned settlements in Delhi and NOIDA navigate courts, bureaucracy, residency/address documentation, and privatized utility rules, its substantive empirical analysis focuses exclusively on housing/land tenure and electricity metering. Water and sewage/sanitation are mentioned only as brief unanalyzed background details, and the authors explicitly state (p. S52, fn. 18) that ongoing projects for access to water and sewage disposal are left as an open question for now.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Fails Criterion 2 under both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, the study does not empirically examine any rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, official discretion, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). While a brief subsection on illegal water connections notes a grievance cell, penalties, and lack of metering/field audits, that discussion is descriptive background drawing on media reports rather than an empirically analysed exposure. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, although the paper invokes 'urban water governance', inadequate municipal funds, and provider management challenges as macro-background and tabulates public water schemes operated by different municipal/state bodies, its actual study design and empirical exposure examine physical water infrastructure (obsolete vs. newly commissioned plants, capacity gaps, pipe leakages/bursts) and spatial geography (distance and slope/elevation from service reservoirs across Zones I, II, and III), rather than a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor.
rationale: This empirical geography study surveys 506 connected households across 25 urban water supply schemes in Guwahati, India, and tests tap-water samples to assess household water security (quantity, quality, reliability, coping strategies, and accessibility). Although it clearly examines household water service access (C1) with empirical household outcomes (C3, C4), its analysed exposures are physical infrastructure attributes (obsolete vs. newly commissioned plants, capacity gaps, pipe leakages/bursts) and spatial geography (distance and slope from service reservoirs across Zones I, II, and III). References to urban water governance, municipal funding shortages, and media-reported water theft/lack of metering serve only as unanalysed background context rather than an empirically studied legal, administrative, regulatory, or governance mechanism (failing C2 under both the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading and the plain reading). Excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure).

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 because it examines governance, institutional, and policy factors (World Bank/IMF structural adjustment and PRSP conditionalities, transnational water policy networks, and public-to-private utility shifts). However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading because its central analytical focus is macro-governance ideology and elite transnational policy networking ('green neoliberalism' and global policy forums such as the WWC, WCW, and WBCSD), rather than investigating how a specific rule-type mechanism directly governs household or community service access (tariff hikes, prepaid meters, and contract redefinitions are cited only in brief secondary vignettes). Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the paper is still excluded due to lack of empirical methods/evidence on service access (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude).
rationale: Goldman (2007) is a critical political-economy and historical policy essay tracing how the World Bank and elite transnational policy networks (such as the World Water Council, World Commission on Water, WBCSD, and WaterAid) constituted and diffused a global 'green neoliberal' water privatization agenda. It contains no empirical methods section, no defined population or sample, no identifiable empirical study design, and no primary empirical evaluation or systematic synthesis of household or community water/sanitation service access (relying on secondary NGO/media citations and brief unmethodologized footnotes from the 2002 Johannesburg summit). In addition, its core focus is macro-governance and transnational policy-network hegemony rather than a rule-type legal/administrative mechanism governing household service access. Excluded under E05 (no empirical evidence); it would also be excluded under the plain wording of Criterion 2 for failing Criteria 3, 4, and 5.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain/broad wording of Criterion 2, but FAILS the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording ('Examines a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper descriptively examines WUA institutional/governance capacity across eight rural and peri-urban WSSs (staffing/plumber counts, volunteer vs. professionalized WUA management, presence of a supplier Water Use Efficiency Programme [WUEP], and self-financing vs. subsidy reliance) alongside socio-economic factors. However, under the active 2026-10-13 narrow clarification, Criterion 2 requires an empirical examination of a rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure governing access). Here, all eight systems are community-managed WUAs, national laws (Law 142 of 1994; Decree 1076 of 2015) appear only as unanalysed macro-governance background, low water prices/billing are mentioned only qualitatively in passing as O&M context rather than analysed as tariff rules governing access, and the empirical explanatory analysis tests socio-economic/demographic factors (household size, education, age, occupation, rural vs. peri-urban distance to Cali) and operational water-conservation/leak-control practices on water use efficiency.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Although the study empirically measures domestic water consumption (lpcd) and system water supply per capita across 965 households and 8 community water supply systems in Colombia, its explanatory focus is on socio-economic/behavioral determinants of water demand efficiency (household size, education, age, occupation, rural vs. peri-urban proximity) and technical/operational system losses. National water regulations (Law 142 of 1994; Decree 1076 of 2015) are cited only as unanalysed background, all eight studied systems share the same WUA ownership form, and descriptive discussions of WUA volunteer staffing, flow metering, and supplier Water Use Efficiency Programmes reflect operational/conservation management capacity rather than a rule-type legal, administrative, tariff, or regulatory mechanism directly governing household service access. Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, the descriptive comparison of WUA governance/management capacity would support inclusion.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 because it examines institutional, fiscal, and administrative governance factors in China (central-local fiscal decentralisation, local tax assignment, extra-budgetary municipal capital financing via land leases/bonds/loans/connection fees, and municipal urban construction bureau autonomy). Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading because it focuses on macro-level intergovernmental fiscal relations and general municipal capital construction financing/administration across bundled urban infrastructure rather than analysing a rule-type mechanism (such as eligibility screening, tenure/documentation rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access.
rationale: Excluded as E05 (no empirical evidence). Wu (1999) is a macro-level policy and institutional overview of urban infrastructure financing and municipal construction administration in post-1979 China, supplemented by an illustrative narrative profile of Shanghai based on secondary literature and published statistical yearbook aggregates (Tables 2, 3, 5, and 6). It has no primary data collection, no identifiable quantitative, qualitative, or socio-legal empirical methodology, and is not a systematic synthesis. In addition, while it satisfies the plain wording of Criterion 2 as an institutional/fiscal governance overview, it fails the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading because it examines intergovernmental fiscal revenue-sharing, capital financing instruments (taxes, land leases, bonds, loans), and municipal capital-budgeting bureaucracy across bundled infrastructure sectors (roads, bridges, subways, gas, water, sewerage) rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access. Because it lacks an empirical method and identifiable study design, plain_criterion2_decision is also exclude.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include) because it examines inclusive municipal governance, gradual institutional change, municipal-NGO-CBO institutional partnerships, and participatory urban planning in Harare. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading (c2_legal_admin_factor = no): the study evaluates a Gates Foundation-funded slum-upgrading project and broad participatory municipal-community partnership primarily aimed at housing delivery, in which reticulated water and sewer pipes were installed as bundled physical project infrastructure. References to rigid town planning standards (as bottlenecks to low-cost housing, with City housing policy not yet revised), incremental housing development, Federation stand-allocation criteria, and two sentences on post-upgrade municipal bill arrears are descriptive housing-project features rather than an empirical analysis of a legal, regulatory, or administrative rule directly governing water or sanitation service access.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the study empirically documents household transitions from shallow wells and pit latrines to reticulated water and sewer infrastructure in Harare's Dzivarasekwa Extension and would be included under the literal broad wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include), its exposure is a donor-funded slum-upgrading project and participatory municipal-community governance partnership focused on housing delivery rather than a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing water or sanitation service access.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Under BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 (any legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory, or governance factor) and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion or accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership or regulatory structure directly governing service access rather than generic project delivery or macro-governance background), eligibility is unclear (cannot_tell) because the full text is not accessible. While the title references local government, public-private partnerships, and multilevel governance issues, the actual mechanism examined cannot be determined without accessible text.
rationale: reason: "full text not accessible". The record has retrieval_status = not_accessible and no full text or abstract is available in the provided input ([FULL TEXT NOT ACCESSIBLE — NO VERIFIED FULL-TEXT PDF OR OA XML COULD BE RETRIEVED]). Per screening rules (zero guessing from title/metadata alone and mandatory handling of inaccessible full texts), neither the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading nor the plain reading of Criterion 2, nor empirical design and access outcomes, can be evaluated, requiring decision = "cannot_tell" and exclusion_code = "NONE".

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it analyses legal, municipal, and community governance of urban water and sanitation. Under the narrow rule-type reading, it directly examines concrete legal and administrative rules governing service access: (1) statutory slum notification requirements under the Maharashtra Slum Areas (Improvement, Clearance and Redevelopment) Act, 1971, governing settlement eligibility for basic amenities; (2) the 1 January 1995 residency cut-off rule and documentary proof requirements for legal municipal water connections; (3) administrative burdens, bureaucratic unresponsiveness, and informal payments/political mediation required even for legally eligible pre-1995 residents in notified settlements to obtain shared MCGM/BMC water connections; (4) municipal enforcement raids cutting off water connections and requiring proof of legality to reconnect; and (5) user-charge/tariff rules, operating-hour restrictions, water shut-offs, and informal lock-and-key access rules governing private, CBO-run, and chawl toilet blocks.
rationale: This nine-month comparative ethnographic study in two Mumbai informal settlements (Rafinagar and Khotwadi) empirically examines how formal legal eligibility rules (slum notification under the 1971 Act and the pre-1995 residency proof cut-off), municipal administrative practices and enforcement raids, and local tariff/access rules for toilet blocks shape household and community access, affordability, continuity, and exclusion in water and sanitation services. It meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type readings of Criterion 2, and as a qualitative socio-legal empirical study it is eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it analyzes municipal/utility water sector governance and cost-recovery reforms. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly examines concrete rule-type mechanisms governing piped water connection access: (1) a mandatory 'beneficiary capital contribution' tariff/cost-recovery rule ($60 to $375 tiered by property dimensions) coupled with monthly late-payment enforcement penalties ($1 to $8/month after the deadline), and (2) documentation and land-tenure eligibility requirements for informal 'revenue layout' properties, including the utility's administrative accommodation/waiver removing formal proof of land tenure as an eligibility prerequisite for a water connection and meter once payment receipts for pipes were shown.
rationale: This mixed-methods empirical study examines household access to piped water in informal peripheral settlements ('revenue layouts') of Bangalore, India under the Greater Bangalore Water and Sanitation Project. It directly investigates rule-type legal and administrative mechanisms governing service access under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2 — specifically upfront capital cost-recovery charges tiered by plot size, monthly late-payment penalties, and land-tenure documentation requirements (including an administrative waiver allowing capital contribution receipts to substitute for formal tenure proof in securing water connections and meters) — and reports quantitative and qualitative evidence on household affordability burdens, eligibility, and piped water availability. All inclusion criteria (c1-c6) are met.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines utility governance, municipal/DWASA planning, and institutional arrangements for extending sewerage to slums. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly empirically examines (1) land tenure, lack of legal registration on government/leased land, and eviction notices governing household/landlord sewerage connection and toilet investment (documentation/tenure requirements), (2) tariff, connection-cost-sharing, and subsidy rules (DWASA uniform tariffs, proposed <=2% income fee cap, income-based/area-based/household-size subsidies, EMI/vouchers) (tariff and cost-recovery rules), and (3) mandatory connection and residency enforcement regulations for households within 100 feet of the main sewer line (enforcement/regulatory rules directly governing connection).
rationale: Full-text qualitative empirical study examining sewerage network access, exclusion, willingness to connect, and affordability in 16 low-income communities in Dhaka, Bangladesh. It meets all review inclusion criteria (c1–c6), including the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, because it empirically investigates how lack of legal land registration/tenure security and eviction notices deter toilet upgrading and sewer connection investment, alongside mandatory connection/residency enforcement rules (within 100 feet of trunk mains) and tariff, connection-cost-sharing, and pro-poor subsidy structures. Qualitative socio-legal/institutional studies with primary empirical data are eligible for systematic review inclusion.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Fails both the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading and the plain wording of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, the study does not examine any rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure rules, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure); instead, its focal exposure is generic large-scale water infrastructure project delivery (arrival of inter-basin water transfer via the São Francisco River Integration Project, PISF) alongside demographic, climatic, hydrological, and physical infrastructure factors in a DPSIR model (Table 1). Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, it also fails because legal, institutional, and governance issues (e.g., weak governance, poor urban planning, master plans, water user associations, and discrepancies with official ANA/SINISA indicators) appear only as unanalysed macro-governance background commentary and policy recommendations rather than an empirically examined governance or institutional exposure.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although this empirical multi-method study measures household water access, supply intermittency, and informal water market costs across small municipalities in Paraíba, Brazil (satisfying c1, c3, c4, c5, and c6), its empirical exposure is generic water transfer infrastructure delivery (the São Francisco River Integration Project, PISF) and demographic, climatic, hydrological, and physical distribution factors within a DPSIR model (Table 1). It does not empirically examine a rule-type legal, administrative, regulatory, or institutional mechanism governing service access, referencing governance and planning only as unanalysed background and policy recommendations.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines post-privatization water regulatory governance, clientelism, and collective regulatory mobilization. Under the narrow rule-type reading, it directly analyzes formal and informal rule-type mechanisms governing service access: privatization concession exclusivity and third-party licensing rules (Certificate of Public Convenience), easing of land-title documentary requirements and connection fees under Manila Water's Tubig Para Sa Barangay (TPSB) program, bulk and retail tariff rules, local legislative enforcement (Taguig Resolution 172 mandating direct connections), conversion of POs into legal cooperatives, and payment accommodation/disconnection discretion.
rationale: This socio-legal empirical study based on nearly two years of ethnographic fieldwork and interviews in Taguig, Metro Manila examines how post-privatization regulatory rules and community/NGO 'regulatory mobilization' shaped household and community piped water access for the urban poor. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain reading and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, directly analyzing concession exclusivity clauses, third-party licensing, easing of land-title documentary requirements and connection fees under the TPSB program, bulk and retail tariff disputes, local council enforcement resolutions, and flexible payment accommodation preventing cut-offs.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it analyses local municipal water/wastewater policies, urban planning governance, intermunicipal utility associations, Veolia's operational concession, and the 2007 Swedish Water Act. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access and cost allocation: (1) statutory full cost-recovery ('principe du prix coûtant'), municipal tariff equalization ('péréquation municipale'), connection fee rules (~70,000 vs. ~150,000 SEK/house), and the 2007 Water Act rule authorizing cost-differentiated intra-municipal tariffs; (2) administrative classification of 122 residential zones into municipal connection versus alternative-system tiers; (3) unanimous co-owner consent requirements and bonus building-right incentives for co-ownership mini-networks (minimum 20 houses); and (4) permitting and enforcement rules, including municipal environmental authorization/registration fees for individual systems, mandatory adequate sanitation upgrades triggered by building-permit applications to convert summerhouses into permanent residences, and statutory municipal obligations to enforce remediation or connect properties when autonomous systems pose environmental hazards.
rationale: This French-language empirical case study (eligible under Criterion 10 with feasible translation from the clean full text) examines household and municipal water and sanitation access across Stockholm County and in Norrtälje, Sweden. It satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2 by analysing statutory full cost-recovery and municipal tariff equalization/differentiation rules under the 2007 Water Act, zone-level connection screening, unanimous co-owner consent and connection-fee rules for co-ownership mini-networks, building-permit sanitation mandates triggered by converting summerhouses to permanent residences, and mandatory municipal connection enforcement when off-network systems cause environmental harm. Drawing on stakeholder interviews, municipal planning records, and Svenskt Vatten (VASS) data, it reports concrete connection coverage, seasonal vs. year-round availability, and tariff/connection-cost outcomes.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Plain reading: examines national drinking water policy (NCWSP), project laws and by-laws, customary local water rights, and pump-community governance. Narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading: directly examines concrete legal and administrative rules governing household water access, including (1) eligibility and cost-recovery rules (the mandatory 5% upfront community capital contribution of two Mio Cedis / approx. US$210 paid to the district to qualify for a pump, plus higher post-hoc buy-in entrance fees when wealthier households pay the contribution on behalf of neighbours, and maintenance water fees), (2) formal registration and membership rules under project law restricting pump use rights to registered members at their place of residence, and (3) local discretion and accommodation (exempting vulnerable houses from entrance and water fees and creating a hierarchy of use rights limiting water quantities and usage for non-members).
rationale: This 4-page qualitative socio-legal article reports empirical findings from the author's 2004-2006 field investigation in a rural Nankan settlement of northern Ghana (citing Eguavoen, 2007) examining how Ghana's National Community Water and Sanitation Program (NCWSP) rules altered local household water rights and access. It satisfies both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 by analyzing specific formal eligibility, cost-recovery, registration/membership, and accommodation rules—including the two Mio Cedis (5%) upfront capital contribution required to qualify, formal pump-community membership boundaries, buy-in entrance fees, exemptions for vulnerable houses, and quantity/usage limits for non-members—and linking them to concrete household access, delay, exclusion, and source-substitution outcomes. Although specific data-collection instruments and sample counts are not detailed in this short article, the empirical field investigation, population, rule-type exposures, and access outcomes are clearly identifiable, and qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for the mechanism synthesis.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain/literal wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor') because it examines institutional mandates under the Local Government Act and Water Works Act, dissolution of Karonga Town Council in 2009, incomplete decentralization, municipal financing, and the absence of a national WASH law and town by-laws. However, it fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading because it analyzes broad municipal/sector WASH-for-disaster-risk-reduction governance (budget constraints, stakeholder coordination/council bypass, M&E capacity, advocacy, NIMBY/EIA barriers to waste disposal sites, and unregulated yard burials) rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden on users, tenure/documentation rules, tariffs, discretion, or access enforcement).
rationale: Excluded primarily under E03 (Wrong exposure) under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, and secondarily fails Criterion 4 (Wrong outcome). While the study passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 by examining municipal WASH governance, statutory mandates, town council dissolution, incomplete decentralization, and missing WASH legislation/bylaws in Karonga Town, Malawi, it investigates broad sector-level disaster risk reduction governance (council budget shortfalls, NGO coordination/council bypass, M&E capacity, advocacy, solid waste siting, and unregulated yard burials) rather than a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access. Even under the plain reading of Criterion 2, the overall decision remains exclude because the primary empirical study (35 institutional stakeholders) measures stakeholder governance roles, priority rankings, and perceived governance bottlenecks rather than household or community water or sanitation access, connection, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion outcomes (coverage statistics in Section 3.1 are cited strictly from secondary reports, with the drop from 65% to 51% attributed to earthquake and flood damage).

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, it examines EU, national, provincial, and municipal environmental and water governance and legal frameworks. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, it directly analyses concrete rule-type mechanisms governing household sanitation access and service responsibility: the statutory municipal sewer-provision mandate and provincial waiver rule (Section 10.33 of the Dutch Environmental Management Act), experimental regulatory derogations under the Crisis and Recovery Act, mandatory anterior residency agreements requiring plot buyers to self-provide wastewater treatment as a condition of residence, water board discharge permitting rules (requiring Category III OSSFs), compliance inspections/enforcement, pollution vs. sewer cost-recovery levies, and administrative accommodation/reversal restoring municipal sewer connections.
rationale: This socio-legal empirical case study satisfies all systematic review inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. It examines household wastewater/sanitation service provision and municipal sewer connection in Oosterwold (Almere, the Netherlands), analysing concrete legal and regulatory rules governing service access and responsibility (the statutory municipal sewer duty and provincial waiver rules under EMA s. 10.33, Crisis and Recovery Act experimental rules, mandatory anterior residency agreements, water board discharge permits, inspections, and levies) using interviews, document analysis, and water board inspection data (28/40 and 33/199 OSSF failures), culminating in mandatory municipal sewer connections for non-compliant and future households.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading: under the plain wording, it examines legal, regulatory, institutional, and governance factors shaping WASH disparities; under the narrow rule-type reading, it specifically discusses rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access, including municipal incorporation/underbounding boundaries, full-cost recovery tariff structures and disconnection for non-payment, linking service provision to property ownership/tenure, and criminalisation of open defecation and septic non-compliance.
rationale: Although this Lancet Global Health Review directly addresses household and community water and sanitation access (c1) and discusses rule-type legal, regulatory, and tariff/tenure mechanisms governing access under both the plain and narrow readings of Criterion 2 (c2), it is a thematic narrative and policy review rather than an original empirical study or a systematic empirical synthesis (c3 = no). It collects no primary data and applies no systematic screening, extraction, or synthesis methodology, relying on illustrative secondary examples and the authors' collective experiences. Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence).

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain reading, the study examines multi-level water governance, regional autonomy, and institutional fragmentation across 11 government departments. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it empirically examines concrete regulatory and administrative mechanisms directly governing service access and allocation: non-enforcement of mandatory commercial groundwater extraction permits and metering, bureaucratic discretion and tariff-classification loopholes (exempting 'warung' and misclassifying commercial resorts as residential 'villas' to pay lower water tariffs), PDAM public-private partnership/part-privatization under Law No. 7 of 2004, Governor Decree No. 16 Year 2009 water tariff hikes and non-payment, and unaffordable household piped-water connection fees and utility waiting lists.
rationale: This empirical multi-method political ecology case study examines household and community water access and equity in Bali, Indonesia. It investigates specific rule-type legal, regulatory, tariff, and utility-governance mechanisms directly affecting household water access—including non-enforcement of groundwater extraction permits and metering, discretionary exemptions and tariff misclassification ('villa' vs. hotel rates), 11-department and Regency-level regulatory fragmentation, PDAM part-privatization/commercialization, and unaffordable household piped connection fees—and links them to household exclusion, intermittent piped supply, dry shallow wells, and reliance on unsafe refill water. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings of Criterion 2.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, though borderline in quantitative framing. Under the plain wording, the study clearly examines institutional/governance and tenure factors related to municipal utility (BWD) water access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, while the quantitative regressions conceptualize BWD connection status and homeownership as household physical resources rather than isolating a legal rule, the primary qualitative empirical component (Aim 2, n = 18 interviews plus BWD personnel inquiry, pp. 505-506) directly examines rule-type mechanisms governing access to a BWD household connection: (1) tariff/cost-recovery rules (PHP 6,000 connection fee plus homeowner responsibility for PHP 4,000-8,000 in meter-to-home piping), (2) discretion/accommodation rules (an installment payment plan requiring PHP 3,000 down and PHP 3,000 over 3 months, granted on a case-by-case basis with low public awareness), and (3) administrative burden and informal rent-seeking in application processing (needing to regularly follow up and 'be annoyingly persistent,' plus reported 'under the table' payments). Per the qualitative socio-legal safeguard, these empirical mechanism findings support inclusion.
rationale: This mixed-methods empirical study in urban Baguio City, Philippines (N = 396 household surveys; n = 18 in-depth interviews) examines household water service access, consumption, perceived cleanliness, ease of access, and affordability. Although the quantitative regression models focus primarily on household financial, physical, and social resources (modeling homeownership and BWD utility connection status as physical resources), Aim 2's qualitative empirical analysis directly investigates rule-type utility mechanisms governing access to a BWD municipal connection—specifically upfront connection fees and piping cost-allocation rules (PHP 6,000 + PHP 4,000-8,000), a strict installment payment plan granted only on a discretionary case-by-case basis with low household awareness, and administrative burdens/informal payment pressures during application follow-up. Under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (together with the safeguard retaining empirical qualitative mechanism evidence), the study meets all inclusion criteria.

rationale: Excluded at full text (E04: Wrong outcome). c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. Under the plain wording, the study analyses the legal, institutional, and governance performance of community-managed Drinking Water Users' Associations (DWUAs) and water cooperatives under Nepal's Water Resource Act 1992, Drinking Water Regulation 1998, and Local Self Governance Act 1999. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, while much of the narrative addresses general WUA management, source maintenance, and corruption in pump repairs, the paper also empirically examines specific rule-type mechanisms directly governing household service access: (1) utility ownership and regulatory structure (autonomous statutory DWUAs/cooperatives operating under their own constitutions independently of municipal regulatory scrutiny); (2) tariff and connection-charge rules without pro-poor subsidies (NPR 50,000 / USD 440 upfront fee for a new tap connection, forcing agrarian/poor households to pool funds for shared taps, plus volumetric tariff hikes from NPR 20 to NPR 80 per 6,000 litres); (3) administrative rationing, moratoria on new tap applications (no new taps registered in Tansen since 1994; authorities refusing applications), and 11-year waiting queues in Bartung WUA alongside discretionary/corrupt queue-jumping for applicants paying double (NPR 100,000 / USD 880); and (4) registration rules requiring taps to be registered in male counterparts' names, barring women from association membership.
rationale: This comparative mixed-methods empirical study of 350 households and qualitative focus group discussions in two Nepalese municipalities (Tansen and Damauli) meets all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Beyond general operational management, it directly examines utility ownership and regulatory structure (statutory DWUAs/cooperatives operating autonomously without municipal oversight) alongside concrete rule-type access barriers: freezes on new tap applications, high upfront connection charges (NPR 50,000) without pro-poor subsidies forcing shared-tap pooling, 11-year connection queues bypassed by informal double payments (NPR 100,000), tariff increases, and male-name tap registration rules excluding women, linked to empirical outcomes on piped connection access, supply duration, continuity, consumption (lpcd), and affordability.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it specifically analyzes statutory land-use, zoning, and tenure/landownership rules under the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act (1976) Development Plan-Town Planning Scheme (DP-TPS) mechanism (where retaining agricultural zoning bars TPS implementation and piped water infrastructure, TPS rules engage only legal landowners rather than informal occupiers or illegal subdivisions, municipal property tax collection is delinked from tenure status, planning authorities exercise regulatory discretion and selective accommodation via overlay zones or modified planning norms, and Gujarat High Court public interest litigation orders enforce municipal water provision) that directly govern whether neighborhoods can legally receive municipal piped water infrastructure and supply.
rationale: This empirical qualitative socio-legal case study (24 months of fieldwork in Ahmedabad, 2016–2018) investigates how statutory land-use zoning, landownership/tenure requirements, administrative discretion and selective accommodation, landowner legal contestations, and High Court judicial directives under the Gujarat Town Planning and Urban Development Act (1976) Development Plan–Town Planning Scheme (DP–TPS) mechanism directly govern the extension of trunk infrastructure, water distribution stations, and legal access to piped municipal water supply in Makhtampura and Sarkhej wards. It satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2, and per review safeguards, qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are included for mechanism synthesis.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines legal, legislative, regulatory, and water-district governance factors shaping colonias water access. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading, it specifically analyzes concrete legal and regulatory rules directly governing utility/district service boundaries, eligibility, tenure/documentation, procedural notice, and utility regulatory structure: (1) the 1971 Texas statute (Article 8280-3.2) empowering Water Control and Improvement District (WCID) boards to unilaterally de-annex 'urban property' explicitly amended to capture unplatted/unrecorded colonias subdivisions; (2) Texas Water Code freeholder (landownership) requirements for water-district candidacy and franchise; (3) English-only courthouse/newspaper constructive notice rules for de-annexation hearings; and (4) judicial and statutory classification of WCID regulatory mandates as narrow special-purpose irrigation districts (followed by formal conversion into Irrigation Districts) exempting them from providing treated domestic water service. Plain=yes and Narrow=yes.
rationale: This full-text peer-reviewed empirical socio-legal / critical legal geography study meets all inclusion criteria (c1-c6). Using primary legislative archives, MALDEF Special Collections litigation archives (stipulations of fact, hearing transcripts, briefs, correspondence), court records, and district personnel communication, Jepson (2012) examines how concrete statutory and regulatory rules—specifically Texas's 1971 unilateral de-annexation statute expanded to cover unplatted colonias subdivisions, freeholder/landownership requirements under the Texas Water Code, constructive notice rules, and special-purpose district regulatory classification—directly governed territorial exclusion of colonias from Water Control and Improvement Districts and foreclosed treated domestic water provision. Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies with clear archival data and rule-type mechanisms directly governing service access and exclusion are explicitly eligible for inclusion in the systematic review.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies both the plain wording of Criterion 2 and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading. rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain = yes) because it examines community-based institutional governance and management of a village water supply by a registered grassroots women's organisation (Vishaka Women's Society). rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, community-based governance by a registered women's society qualifies as an institutional/governance factor and the paper would be included. c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, the study clearly examines legal, administrative, institutional, and governance factors shaping public toilet access (municipal austerity cuts, fragmented borough governance, and the 'ungoverning' of sanitation). rationale: This qualitative empirical study of public sanitation in London satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Using 35 interviews and meeting observations, it examines how the non-statutory legal status of municipal public toilets, pay-per-use cross-subsidy tariff structures, poorly monitored Community Toilet rules (including unauthorized purchase requirements), and frontline discretionary gatekeeping despite statutory/pandemic worker-access documentation shape sanitation availability, affordability, and exclusion for delivery workers and residents with chronic health conditions.

Under the plain wording of Criterion 2 ('a legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this study qualifies ('yes') because it explicitly investigates formal and informal utility 'institutions' (defined via STS/Geels 2004 as planning priorities, engineering design standards, internal capital budgeting, operational production targets, and pump/valve/maintenance practices) shaping uneven water distribution by Lilongwe Water Board (LWB). Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, however, it fails ('no' -> E03 Wrong exposure): the mechanisms empirically unpacked in Sections 5.1-5.5 are infrastructure master-plan delays, hydraulic engineering sizing calculations and construction material choices (2.8% population growth assumption, 50% vs 70% reservoir sizing standard, steel panels vs reinforced concrete), piecemeal capital project implementation, physical plant/pump/valve hydraulic operations (a 100,000 m3/day plant production target and informal pump-operator prioritisation conditioned on physical pipe/reservoir capacity), and deferred pipe maintenance bottlenecks. Although frontline operator pumping/valve discretion (Section 5.4) and brief mentions of private pipe-extension connection costs (fn. 8) and donor reluctance in unplanned settlements (Section 5.3) touch adjacent institutional issues, the paper does not empirically examine a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household/community service access (such as eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, legal/administrative accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure).
rationale: Tiwale (2019) is an empirical qualitative socio-technical case study (54 semi-structured interviews, operational observations, and engineering/operational document analysis) of uneven piped and kiosk water supply in Chikungu, Area 38, Lilongwe, Malawi. Under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2, the study would be included because it examines utility institutional and governance practices shaping service continuity and availability. Under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2, however, it is excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure): what the author terms 'institutions' (following STS/Geels 2004) are infrastructure capital-planning delays, hydraulic engineering sizing assumptions and tank construction standards, piecemeal project delivery, plant/pump/valve hydraulic operating practices, and deferred physical pipe maintenance rather than legal, regulatory, or administrative rule-type mechanisms directly governing household or community service access (such as eligibility rules, tenure/documentation requirements, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, legal/administrative accommodation, enforcement, or regulatory/ownership structure). c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Satisfies BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, it examines legal, administrative, institutional and governance centralisation of urban water and sanitation. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading, rather than unanalysed macro-governance background or generic project delivery, it directly examines utility ownership and statutory/regulatory structure governing service access: specifically, the 9 May 2005 ministerial directive transferring municipal water and sanitation utilities and infrastructure at zero cost to a central parastatal (ZINWA, under the ZINWA Act) in contravention of Sections 168 and 183 of the Urban Councils Act, Bulawayo's retention of municipal utility ownership, the split regulatory structure assigning water production/supply to ZINWA while leaving retail water billing with local authorities, bulk water tariff hikes and ministerial debt-cancellation orders, inter-jurisdictional connection-approval rules (refusal by Harare and Ruwa councils to recognise a ZINWA-approved water connection for Rockview Park after the 1 February 2009 reversal), and the 2009 decentralisation directive returning utility operations to urban councils.
rationale: Full-text qualitative socio-legal/institutional empirical study matching record metadata (Muchadenyika & Williams 2018, DOI 10.1080/03057070.2018.1500748). Although half of the paper examines vehicle licensing (ZINARA), pages 838–844 specifically examine urban water and sanitation service access in Zimbabwe under both the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. It empirically analyses utility ownership and regulatory structure directly governing service access—specifically the extra-statutory 9 May 2005 ministerial directive transferring municipal water and sewerage utilities to the state parastatal ZINWA against Sections 168 and 183 of the Urban Councils Act, Bulawayo's retention of municipal ownership, the split regulatory mandate between ZINWA production/supply and municipal billing, tariff hikes and ministerial bill-scrapping orders, jurisdictional refusal to recognise a ZINWA-approved housing water connection after the 2009 handover, and resulting household water rationing, continuity collapse, potable water access changes and affordability impacts, supported by 30 primary interviews and official audit/parliamentary evidence.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2. Under the plain wording, the study examines legal, institutional, regulatory, and governance factors shaping urban WASH delivery in Beira (Water Law, National Water Policy, draft Water and Sanitation Law, inter-agency governance, and community participation). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 clarification, although framed within a five-dimensional sustainability assessment, the study directly empirically examines rule-type mechanisms governing service access and continuity: (1) utility ownership/delegated management and regulatory/statutory mandate allocation across AdRC (operating under delegated management from FIPAG), AIAS, SASB, CRA, and the Beira Municipal Council directly governing repair responsibility and complaint resolution; (2) formal/legal recognition of community water committees governing self-managed standpipes and user-fee reinvestment (formally recognised by FIPAG in Ponta Gêa vs. lacking legal recognition in Chipangara and Macuti); and (3) tariff and cost-recovery rules, including social tariffs that do not cover operational costs, weak payment enforcement, and billing households without piped water delivery.
rationale: This qualitative phenomenological study (policy review plus 6 semi-structured interviews with utility/agency officials and neighbourhood leaders in Beira, Mozambique) satisfies all inclusion criteria under both the plain and narrow 2026-10-13 readings. Beyond general climate and maintenance themes, it empirically investigates rule-type institutional, regulatory, and tariff mechanisms directly governing household and standpipe service access and continuity: overlapping statutory/operational mandates across delegated utility AdRC (under FIPAG), AIAS, SASB, CRA, and the Municipality that stall breakdown repairs and complaint handling; formal/legal recognition of community committees managing standpipes and user fees (recognised by FIPAG in Ponta Gêa vs. unrecognised in Chipangara and Macuti); and tariff/cost-recovery rules (social tariffs below operational cost, weak payment enforcement, and continued billing during year-long piped water outages). Qualitative socio-legal empirical studies are eligible for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: PASSES PLAIN WORDING / FAILS NARROW 2026-10-13 RULE-TYPE READING. Under the literal plain wording of Criterion 2 ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), this study would qualify (plain_criterion2_decision = 'include') because it examines local municipal water governance and an institutional conflict/negotiation between the elected Municipality Council and the customary Council of Elders within New Caledonia's post-Noumea Agreement decolonization framework. Under the active 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism clarification, however, Criterion 2 is 'no': the paper does not study a rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation/tenure requirements for service connection, tariff or cost-recovery rules governing user access, administrative discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure). Instead, it analyzes political and indigenous contestation around generic capital-works project delivery/staging (2000-2004 vs. 2005-2009 Development Contracts) and rejected tribal demands for bulk water extraction royalties as a window onto political cleavages within Kanak nationalism (exclude as E03).
rationale: This political anthropology article uses a local dispute over the construction and routing of a municipal drinking-water pipeline (AEP Grombaou) in Kone, New Caledonia, to examine emerging ideological cleavages between pro-independence FLNKS elected officials and customary/'indigenous' Kanak activists. While the ethnography touches on community water supply delivery and passes the literal broad wording of Criterion 2 (institutional/governance conflict between municipal and customary authorities, hence plain_criterion2_decision = 'include'), it fails the active 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism scope of Criterion 2. The study examines political mobilization around phased public-works infrastructure delivery (2000-2004 vs. 2005-2009 Development Contracts) and rejected tribal demands for bulk resource extraction royalties rather than any legal, administrative, or regulatory rule-type mechanism directly governing household or community service access (excluded as E03, Wrong exposure).

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes the plain wording of Criterion 2 (plain=yes) because it examines local multi-level water governance, institutional coordination across communities, Gram Panchayats, and Block administration, community participation in O&M, and political patronage/corruption in rural water supply. Fails the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading (narrow=no) because its focus is generic rural water project delivery, infrastructure vs. O&M action prioritization, community-management participation gaps, and broad physical/financial/technical implementation barriers rather than analysing a specific rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff/cost-recovery rules, utility regulatory structure, or formal enforcement/accommodation rules) directly governing household service access. Incidental descriptive mentions of rigid borehole depth budgets, informal village tap turn-taking in one village, patronage in siting/beneficiary lists, and lack of fiscal spending rules illustrate general scheme delivery challenges rather than a studied rule-type access mechanism.
rationale: This qualitative multi-actor empirical study examines rural household and agricultural water security across 16 villages and 6 Blocks in Purulia district, West Bengal, India. While it satisfies Criteria 1, 3, 4, 5, and 6 and would be included under the plain broad wording of Criterion 2 (as an empirical study of local rural water governance, community management, and institutional coordination), it fails the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading of Criterion 2 and is therefore excluded as E03 (Wrong exposure). Rather than evaluating a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household service access (such as eligibility rules, documentation/tenure requirements, tariffs, regulatory structure, or formal enforcement/discretion rules), the paper elicits stakeholder rankings of infrastructure/O&M project-delivery priorities and general financial, hydrogeological, technical, and community-participation barriers.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Fails under the active 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type reading, though passes (borderline) under the literal/plain broad wording of Criterion 2 (plain_criterion2_decision = include, narrow decision = exclude). Under the plain broad wording ('legal, administrative, institutional, regulatory or governance factor'), the paper empirically examines the municipal utility's (NCWSC's) administrative water rationing schedules across residential categories (2016-2018, Table 3), municipal land-use/distribution planning categories (1985 vs 2018, Table 2), and utility non-revenue water losses. Under the 2026-10-13 narrow rule-type clarification, however, no rule-type mechanism directly governing service access (eligibility screening, administrative burden, documentation or tenure requirements, tariff or cost-recovery rules, discretion/accommodation, enforcement, or utility ownership/regulatory structure) is empirically analysed as an exposure: NCWSC's residential classification is explicitly used and validated as a proxy for neighbourhood socio-economic status alongside satellite-derived settlement age and population count in the regression model; weekly rationing hours reflect operational drought supply management rather than legal/regulatory eligibility or tariff rules; security of tenure is used only in a descriptive cross-tabulation (Table 1A) to validate the socio-economic proxy; static 2015-2018 tariffs and unenforced kiosk retail rates are described only as study-setting context; and governance appears only as a general policy recommendation.
rationale: Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure) per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. While the study empirically examines household/itinerary-level piped water consumption and sufficiency in Nairobi from 2008 to 2018 (satisfying C1, C3, C4, C5, and C6), its analytical exposures are socio-economic and spatial-demographic factors: the utility's residential classification (explicitly validated against household survey data as a proxy for neighbourhood socio-economic status), Landsat-derived neighbourhood settlement age, and itinerary population count, alongside descriptive operational data on weekly water rationing hours and non-revenue water losses. It does not empirically evaluate a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access (such as eligibility screening, documentation or tenure rules, administrative burden, tariff/cost-recovery rules, enforcement, discretion, or utility ownership/regulatory structure); tariffs, unenforced kiosk rates, and tenure are mentioned only as background context or SES proxy validation, and governance is invoked only as a general policy recommendation. Under the broad literal wording of Criterion 2, the descriptive analysis of NCWSC's administrative rationing schedules and municipal residential planning categories would support inclusion (plain_criterion2_decision = include).

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Passes BOTH the plain wording and the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type reading of Criterion 2 (with a borderline note on framing). Under the plain wording, it clearly examines municipal utility governance, organizational culture/values, regulatory pressures, and CAP administration. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, although the overarching theoretical construct is organizational values (Schwartz human values typology), the empirical analysis directly examines how core rule-type mechanisms govern affordability and access to relief: tariff and cost-recovery rules (ascending block rates, strict rate uniformity, refusal to abate principal charges even on leaks, consultant rate benchmarking, state regulatory agency rate approvals, and Safe Drinking Water Act compliance cost pass-through), street-level discretion and accommodation (waiving interest/fees, flex-pay payment plans, principal debt erasure, ad-hoc hardship grants), eligibility screening and administrative burden in CAPs (differential discounts by senior/low-income status, simplified enrollment, outreach clinics), enforcement (aggressive collections, fines, liens, shutoffs), and perceived municipal legal constraints on differential pricing.
rationale: This qualitative socio-legal empirical study (33 interviews with 37 officials/staff across 11 municipal water utilities in Massachusetts and Pennsylvania) satisfies all inclusion criteria for the systematic review's mechanism synthesis. Although framed around organizational values (Schwartz's typology), it empirically examines concrete rule-type mechanisms under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope — including tariff and cost-recovery rules (ascending block rates, strict uniform pricing, non-abatement of principal charges even for leaks, consultant benchmarking, and state regulatory rate filings), street-level discretion and accommodation (waiving fees/interest, flex-pay plans, principal debt erasure, hardship grants), CAP eligibility discounts and enrollment outreach, perceived legal constraints on differential rates, and punitive collection enforcement — and links them to utility-level water affordability and relief/exclusion practices across the 11 cities. Confidence is rated medium because the primary explanatory lens is organizational culture/values and outcomes are captured at the utility policy/practice level rather than direct household-level affordability or shutoff rates.

c2_plain_vs_narrow_note: Under the plain wording of Criterion 2, this study WOULD satisfy Criterion 2 because it examines legal, procedural, and institutional governance factors (the National Water Act 1998 including 'existing lawful use' entitlements tied to irrigated land ownership, the National Water Resource Strategy 2, DWAF 2007 WUA establishment procedural guidelines, and institutional power asymmetries). Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type clarification, Criterion 2 is NOT met because these rules and governance processes do not directly govern household or community water or sanitation service access; instead, the paper examines stakeholder power asymmetries in establishing an IWRM collaborative institution (an agricultural WUA) for bulk irrigation/productive water resources. Because Criterion 1 and Criterion 4 also fail, plain_criterion2_decision remains exclude.
rationale: Excluded (E07 - Wrong service, corresponding to Exclusion Criterion 7: water-resource studies unrelated to household or community service access). Although the paper is an empirical qualitative case study examining South African water law and institutional governance, it investigates IWRM stakeholder participation and power asymmetries in attempting to establish an agricultural Water User Association governing dam/canal water for productive irrigation purposes, not household or community drinking-water or sanitation service access. Municipal drinking water is mentioned only once in passing as background context. Even under the plain broad reading of Criterion 2, the study remains excluded because it fails Criteria 1 and 4.
